summary: Full audit of pages #21-#24 completed. Root cause of #21's 96.3% bounce / 0s TOP diagnosed: the published artifact is a 418-byte alias redirect stub (noindex + meta-refresh) because content/blog/why-your-electric-bill-keeps-rising-2026.md has `draft: true` in frontmatter — there is NO content at the URL, so instant exits are structurally guaranteed. #24's 36% bounce outlier is explained by an action-first first screen (the Quick Answer IS the executable instruction), numbered steps, contextual affiliate placement after free actions, and strong query-to-content match. #22's residentially-hedged demand-charge framing is correct and DOU-supported. All EPA claims on #23/#24 verified against live EPA pages (retrieved 2026-08-29). Per-page OUTPUT CONTRACT blocks and exact weak-copy quotes included below.
findings: OUTPUT CONTRACT #21 (why-your-electric-bill-keeps-rising-2026) — VERDICT: CRITICAL DEFECT, not a copy problem. URL: https://utilityexplained.com/blog/why-your-electric-bill-keeps-rising-2026/ (retrieved 2026-08-29). Frontmatter title/meta: title="Why your electric bill keeps rising: Complete Guide (2026)", description="Learn everything about why your electric bill keeps rising in 2026. Costs, comparisons, expert tips for US homeowners." — neither is ever seen by a reader because the page does not publish. Evidence: public/blog/why-your-electric-bill-keeps-rising-2026/index.html is 418 bytes: <!doctype html>...<title>https://utilityexplained.com/blog/why-did-my-utility-bill-go-up-this-month/</title>...<meta name=robots content="noindex">...<meta http-equiv=refresh content="0; url=...why-did-my-utility-bill-go-up-this-month/">. Cause chain: file has `draft: true`; Hugo emits no real page; the target page why-did-my-utility-bill-go-up-this-month.md lists this slug in its `aliases:` array, so Hugo builds the stub in #21's place. Root-cause fix (executable): either (1) remove `draft: true` from #21 so the guide publishes, or (2) if consolidation is intended, delete the `aliases` entry in why-did-my-utility-bill-go-up-this-month.md and instead add "/blog/why-did-my-utility-bill-go-up-this-month/" to an `aliases:` array in #21 — the alias direction is currently inverted and creates a redirect loop hazard.

OUTPUT CONTRACT #21 (continued) — FACT CHECKS (all as of 2026-08-29): VERIFIED: "The American Society of Civil Engineers gives the U.S. electric grid a D+ grade" — https://infrastructurereportcard.org/cat-item/energy/ shows Energy: D+ (2025 Report Card). DOES NOT MATCH/UNVERIFIED: cover page claims "fossil fuels still supply 60% of U.S. electricity in 2026" — https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us.php (retrieved 2026-08-29) reports 58% for 2025, so the 2026 60% figure is unsupported; NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: "over 70% of transmission and distribution lines as nearing or past their design life" (not found on ASCE's current Energy page), "utilities filed 147 rate cases across 48 states" with "average request for a 5.8% rate increase" (no source cited), "Texas ERCOT...$1.85/month", "California...$2.30/month", "22 weather disasters costing over $1 billion each", "38% more heatwaves...47% more flooding events", "EIA estimates climate-related infrastructure investments added 0.8-1.4 cents/kWh". MISATTRIBUTED SOURCE: the only source URL in the RICH text is https://www.eia.gov/TODAYINENERGY/detail.php?id=62303 (in redirect target page's frontmatter) which is a June 2024 EIA piece about slightly-higher summer bills — not 2026-specific and unrelated to the 17.4-cents/kWh / 22.5%-since-2020 / $21-per-month figures on #21's first screen. VERIFIED: "The average household's leaks can waste more than 9,300 gallons" etc. is an EPA fact but does not appear on #21.

...` block starting "Your electric bill keeps rising because of three main factors: rate increases approved by utility commissions, higher fixed charges (delivery/customer fees), and increased consumption from extreme weather." — an un-numerated wall with no citation. OUTPUT CONTRACT #22 (49-demand-charges-electricity-bill-explained) — VERDICT: SOUND, LOW-RISK PAGE; 82.6% bounce is not a defect. OUTPUT CONTRACT #23 (why-did-my-water-bill-suddenly-increase) — VERDICT: EPA-ACCURATE BUT GENERIC ANSWER; 77.8% bounce at 10s TOP from a first screen that states causes but gives no action. URL: https://utilityexplained.com/blog/why-did-my-water-bill-suddenly-increase/ (retrieved 2026-08-29). Title/meta: title "Why Did My Water Bill Suddenly Increase?", description "Understand the most common reasons water bills spike and how to troubleshoot them." — the meta description is the weak point: it promises to "understand" reasons, matching a searcher who wants a diagnosis, but the first visible answer is "A sudden water bill increase usually indicates a leak (toilet, pipe, or irrigation), rate changes, or seasonal usage spikes." — a category list, not the immediate leak-check instruction the searcher needs. EXACT WEAK-QUOTE #2: "If your usage seems to jump without any change in habits, start with a leak check before assuming a billing error." — no concrete step follows this sentence; the first actionable check (food-coloring dye test) is several screenfuls down.

OUTPUT CONTRACT #23 (continued) — FACT CHECKS (retrieved 2026-08-29): ALL VERIFIED against live EPA pages. Source [1] https://www.epa.gov/watersense/fix-leak-week confirms: >9,300 gallons/year average household leaks, ~10% savings from fixing easily corrected leaks, "If a family of four exceeds 12,000 gallons per month, there could be serious leaks", food-coloring dye test with 10-minute bowl check, "a leaky faucet that drips at the rate of one drip per second can waste more than 3,000 gallons per year", "A showerhead leaking at 10 drips per minute wastes more than 500 gallons per year", irrigation leak "1/32nd of an inch... can waste about 6,300 gallons of water per month", and 9% of homes have leaks wasting 50+ gallons/day. Source [2] https://www.epa.gov/watersense/how-we-use-water confirms: "The average American family uses more than 300 gallons of water per day at home. Roughly 70 percent of this use occurs indoors." and "outdoor water use accounts for 30 percent of household use yet can be much higher in drier parts of the country." No fabricated numbers found on this page.

OUTPUT CONTRACT #23 (continued) — OVERLAP MAP (packet question): #23 (why-did-my-water-bill-suddenly-increase), #8 (06-water-bill-too-high, author Tanya Patterson), #4 (water-meter-running-when-no-water-used, author Margaret Harrington) all answer the "water bill went up / high water bill" intent. Boundaries as currently written: #23 = spike-moment diagnosis (causes + how to check yourself), #8 = structured investigation protocol (compare bill, test meter, isolate valve — the most methodical), #4 = running-meter leak localization (main-valve test, inside-vs-outside). The pages cross-link: #23 opens with "For more detail, see common causes of high water bills" pointing to #8; #4's "Estimate the impact" section links to #23. #23 and #4 share EPA Home Maintenance/leak sources; #8 uses different WaterSense pages (Getting Started/Start Saving/Residential Toilets). REAL RISK: #23 and #8 each carry a Quick Answer and overlapping leak-check tables; they are not hard-canonicalized to one another, so three URLs compete for the same SERP intent. RECOMMENDATION: make #8 the canonical "high water bill" investigation URL and point #23 and #4 at it via rel=canonical, OR restructure #23 to own only the 'sudden month-over-month spike' angle (rate/tier/billing-cycle changes) and hand off all leak diagnosis to #8/#4. The Hugo site uses aliases for redirects, so a canon strategy needs a template decision — flag to Commander.

(4) Sections answer the reader's implied next questions ("Why Running Toilets Are Easy to Miss", "How It Shows Up on Your Water Bill", "What to Do After You Confirm a Leak"). (5) FAQ mirrors search-long-tail questions. 36% bounce with 3s TOP is consistent with a scan-and-execute pattern: readers get the answer in the first screenful and leave to do the test — for this page that is success, not a defect.
